editions.title: Microsoft quits Nscale site as AI trade wobbles and iPhone Duo supply strains
editions.intro:
The biggest story is a reported setback for Nscale, the British AI cloud startup. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first UK data centre in Loughton, Essex, weeks before Nscale's planned IPO of up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, and Microsoft has not commented. The report lands as investors grow wary of neocloud firms, and CoreWeave shares were marked down in coverage of the story.

The wider backdrop is a deepening selloff in US tech shares. Bloomberg reports that this is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI "picks and shovels" suppliers, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The FT also argues that America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical constraints. Against that, SemiAnalysis says more than 300 local data-centre moratoriums have delayed only a few projects so far. Meta's earnings, previewed by the FT as a test of confidence in AI spending, are the next major read-across.

Apple dominated the rest of the day's flow. The iPhone Duo, its first foldable, is reportedly sold out into January, with staff told walk-in buyers are unlikely to get stock on launch day, and Gurman calls the staggered pre-order rollout a "major mistake". Apple's EU energy label put the device's battery at 4,883 mAh. Rumours also point to a touchscreen MacBook and a HomeView smart display with a robotic arm, with a possible retail refresh on 6 November. Most of these remain unconfirmed.

top_stories.summary: Apple Store staff reportedly told customers without pre-orders to expect no launch-day stock. Apple says demand is extraordinary, and shipping estimates have slipped to around late January in most countries.

editions.title: Microsoft Walks Away From Nscale Site as Neocloud Nerves Grow
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the day is Microsoft's reported withdrawal from an anchor deal for Nscale's first British data centre in Loughton, Essex. The Telegraph says Microsoft has pulled out weeks before the AI cloud startup's planned IPO, which is reported to seek up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, while Microsoft has not commented. Grid connection delays at the site were also reported, and the story is being read as a sign of wider caution toward neocloud firms.

That caution fed into a broader theme of AI-trade nerves. Bloomberg reports that a deepening selloff in US tech shares is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI supply chain, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The Financial Times, meanwhile, argues America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical limits of power, equipment and money. Investors will look to Meta's earnings next, which the FT frames as a test of whether confidence in the AI spending boom can be restored.

Elsewhere, Ericsson beat expectations with third-quarter adjusted EBITA of SEK 10.1bn against a consensus of SEK 7.93bn, and its shares rose as much as 11% in Stockholm. On the chip front, a single unverified report says Nvidia wants Samsung, Micron and SK hynix to build custom HBM base dies on TSMC's 3nm process, while a separate rumour suggests China could let major firms buy H200 chips under tight caps. Both remain unconfirmed.

editions.title: Nvidia RTX 5090 Row, TSMC Profit Record and Starlink Limits Dominate
editions.intro: TSMC posted a record quarterly profit, with demand for AI chips still far outstripping supply, but it signalled caution on 2027. Meanwhile, the AI trade showed strain: Asian chip suppliers were exposed to a US tech selloff, and reports that OpenAI's revenue trails expectations added to nerves. Ukraine's dispute with SpaceX over Starlink speed limits escalated, with Zelenskyy calling the restrictions deliberate. Apple's iPhone Duo faced shortages and Apple's chief executive called memory supply a crisis.

top_stories.title: TSMC records sixth straight record profit, cautious on 2027
top_stories.summary: TSMC reported record third-quarter net profit of NT$763.1bn, up 69%, with revenue up 51%. It guided to about 44% dollar revenue growth in 2026, but chairman C.C. Wei warned that price-sensitive consumer markets are under pressure and that the company is being prudent about 2027.

top_stories.title: Starshield speed limits cut Ukrainian interceptor drones
top_stories.summary: Speed limits on SpaceX's Starshield network reportedly cut links for interceptor drones above about 161 km/h, forcing Ukrainian units to cancel missions. Reports suggest the order came from the White House or was discussed by Musk and Trump, but these claims are unverified.

top_stories.title: Apple's Ternus calls memory shortage a crisis
top_stories.summary: Apple's chief executive told TIME that memory chip constraints are a crisis and all options should be considered. The comments follow a report that Apple tested memory chips from a Chinese firm, which prompted US warnings against them.

top_stories.title: Microsoft plans multi-gigawatt Maia 300 rollout
top_stories.summary: Microsoft plans to scale its Maia accelerators to multi-gigawatt deployments from 2027, with Maia 300 as its primary inference system. Analysts expect Maia to be only about 10% of its AI chip spend by early 2027, so Nvidia's position is not yet under threat.

top_stories.title: Intel confirms Razor Lake-AX timing and 700 TOPS target
top_stories.summary: Intel SVP Cho Min-sung confirmed Nova Lake for 2027 and Razor Lake-AX for 2028, the latter targeting 700 TOPS of AI compute. The aim is premium devices and physical AI.

top_stories.title: Tesla shows fan-powered Roadster, production 2028
top_stories.summary: Tesla demonstrated its next-generation Roadster using powered fans and a retractable rear wing for downforce. Musk said production begins in 2028, with reservations open at $50,000 for the base model and $250,000 for the Thrust trim.

rumour_watch.note: A reported $20bn revenue shortfall at OpenAI, relayed without a named source. Plausible given the market backdrop, but it is an internal figure and OpenAI has not confirmed it.
Nvidia's Jeff Fisher reportedly denied the RTX 5090 is discontinued, citing tight supply. Credible on the record, but retailer listings at inflated prices suggest supply is genuinely thin.
Reported FTC demands aimed at OpenAI and Anthropic. Only a feed summary, and the story stresses it is not a finding of wrongdoing, so treat as unconfirmed.
DeepSeek says its new Flash model beats larger rivals on agentic tasks. Weights are public, but independent benchmarks are still pending.

Anduril opens a $1.3bn employee tender at a $90bn valuation, up from $61bn in May.
Berkshire Hathaway buys a further $330m of Bending Spoons shares, lifting its stake to about 4%.
Netflix names Peter Rice chief content officer as Bela Bajaria leaves, a day after a 6% staff cut.
Meta removes contested scraping language from its commercial terms after criticism from publishers and experts.

Finance.title: AI trade selloff spreads to Asia as rate fears mount
Finance.notification: Chip rout deepens: US semiconductor index down about 16%, and the selloff has reached Asia's AI supply chain.
Finance.summary:
The dominant story is a sharp reversal in artificial intelligence trades. US technology shares suffered an eight-session rout, the longest since 2008, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell about 16 percent. The selloff has spread to Asia's AI supply chain, with a Goldman Sachs basket of regional AI hardware stocks down 11 percent last week. Investors fear that rising borrowing costs could curb the data-centre spending that has powered the rally, and analysts warn of financing strain at hyperscalers and neoclouds such as CoreWeave, which could reduce orders for TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix. Some investors still see strong demand.

The wider backdrop is a jump in inflation and rates. US September CPI rose 3.7 percent year on year, the VIX climbed about 30 percent in the week to above 21, and the Nasdaq fell 4.48 percent. The 10-year Treasury yield has moved above 5 percent for the first time in almost two decades. Oil has also risen to around US$110 a barrel as Middle East tensions, including Iranian mine attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, add pressure.

Commentators are split on what comes next. Some see fear fading after a sharp Friday volatility spike, while Michael Burry warns of a drift lower in the broader market. Europe's bond market is also under strain, with France braced for a debt sell-off after violent protests.

points.text: Options traders are positioning for a higher VIX as inflation and AI jitters unsettle US stocks.
French bond yields may jump up to 0.1 points on Monday after violent protests and a fragile budget.
Michael Burry warns 55% of S&P 500 stocks are in bear markets, comparing the setup with March 2000.
UK inflation data could decide whether the Bank of England delivers a November rate hike.
Indonesian stocks suffered their worst day since 1998 after an MSCI downgrade warning.
Oil futures rose on Middle East and Russia-Ukraine tensions, feeding energy shares.

World.title: France unrest spreads as protest riots hit Paris and beyond
World.notification: Riots and looting across France after cost-of-living protests; Macron due to address the nation.
World.summary:
France dominates the world news picture today. Student-led and cost-of-living protests turned violent on Saturday, with burnt-out cars and smashed shopfronts in Paris, a historic town hall in Limoges largely destroyed by fire, and about 1,800 to over 2,000 arrests reported. Traders' unions say around 1,500 businesses were damaged, with losses in the hundreds of millions of euros. Interior ministry and union attendance figures differ sharply, and politicians are trading blame months before presidential elections. The government holds a crisis meeting on Monday and Macron is due to address the nation. Calls for the interior minister to resign show the political fallout is widening.

The unrest is feeding into a wider wave of housing and living-cost protests that has reached Italy, Portugal and Albania. Albania's capital has seen days of clashes over university conditions and calls for the prime minister to resign, while Milan and Lisbon have also seen tensions. For markets, the French domestic story is the main concern: the CAC 40 has been weaker, and the euro dipped on the day, although the scale of any lasting economic effect is not yet clear.

Elsewhere, the Ukraine war is escalating on energy targets. Ukrainian drones hit oil terminals and depots in St Petersburg after an energy ceasefire brokered by the US quickly broke down, and oil prices firmed. Trump has paused a sweeping new Russia sanctions package for 60 days, a move criticised by lawmakers from both parties. Middle East and Gulf tensions, including Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, also add to energy-price pressure.

points.text: Politicians from left and right call for interior minister Laurent Nuñez to resign after the government was caught off guard.
Protests over housing and living costs have spread to Milan and Lisbon, where a tent camp has been set up in Rossio Square.
Rubio says Trump's 60-day waiver of Russia sanctions lets the administration assess economic effects, including energy price pressures.
Two killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine trade strikes on energy infrastructure after the energy ceasefire collapsed.
Taiwan says it drove away 16 Chinese vessels in simultaneous maritime harassment, calling it hybrid warfare.
Tirana protests enter a sixth day; 272 people injured since Tuesday, including 169 police officers, as Rama refuses to resign.

Tech.title: Microsoft quits Nscale UK site as AI cloud IPO nears
Tech.notification: Microsoft reportedly pulls out of Nscale's UK data centre weeks before its IPO. Nscale says it remains committed.
Tech.summary:
The biggest story in tech today is a reported setback for Nscale, the British AI cloud startup. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first UK data centre in Loughton, Essex, just weeks before Nscale's planned IPO, which seeks up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong. Microsoft has not commented, and the site has already faced grid connection delays.

The episode lands amid wider unease about AI spending. Several items point the same way: a deepening selloff in US tech shares is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI supply chain, where rising financing costs could curb data centre and hardware spending. Investor caution around neocloud firms is also part of the Nscale story. Separately, reports that OpenAI's $500bn Stargate project has hit turbulence, and that OpenAI now plans to spend $600bn on AI infrastructure through 2030 rather than $1.4tn, add to the sense that the build-out is being recalibrated.

Other threads include Apple's iPhone Duo, its first foldable, where Mark Gurman says the company made a major mistake by opening pre-orders in more than 70 countries at once, and shipping dates have slipped to around January. Rumours about Apple's touchscreen MacBook and a robotic HomeView also circulated. Meanwhile, Meta's earnings are previewed as a test of confidence in the AI boom.

Fashion.title: Chanel's Wuhan store, McQueen exit and luxury's slowing US demand
Fashion.notification: Chanel opens its first Wuhan store at SKP as McQueen's creative director leaves after three years.
Fashion.summary:
Chanel has revealed a hoarding for its first Wuhan boutique at the SKP department store, where it will sit on the K Avenue promenade between Louis Vuitton and Cartier. The store will be Chanel's second in the Hubei region and its 13th in China. Celine, Giorgio Armani and Prada are also set to open at SKP Wuhan, timed with the WWD x SKP Global Fashion & Beauty Summit. The move reflects luxury brands in China adjusting to a prolonged market reset by closing weaker stores and testing new regional markets.

Leadership is the other big theme. Seán McGirr is leaving Alexander McQueen after three years, with his Spring/Summer 2027 London show as his final collection. He has not announced his next role and the house has not named a successor, leaving the Kering-owned label in transition. Separately, Veronica Leoni is reported to be leaving Calvin Klein after four seasons, though details are sparse, and a New York Times piece asks who should fill the open creative roles at Calvin Klein and McQueen.

The sector mood is less upbeat. Business of Fashion headlines point to weak numbers, empty chairs and a possible loss of momentum in US demand, which has been a key lifeline for luxury. Those items give few specifics, but together they suggest pressure on performance and management across the big groups. Elsewhere, Cartier's second Choeur des Pierres chapter in Kyoto and Victoria's Secret's Pink taking the halftime slot added brighter, more consumer-facing notes.

points.text: McGirr's McQueen exit closes a three-year tenure that brought the house back to London with a younger, club-influenced approach.

Cartier unveiled 46 new high jewellery pieces in Kyoto, with the Stellara necklace, worn by Jisoo, as the highlight.
